# Current from key to starter solenoid: sizing your immobilizer relay

Installing a starter motor immobilizing relay inline between the ignition switch and the starter solenoid is a common strategy for securing vehicles against hot-wiring or unauthorized starting attempts. The critical design decision here isn't just about adding a relay; it's about correctly identifying the load that specific wire carries so you don't underspecify your switching component.

You mentioned considering the MAH-112-C-4, which boasts a 30A switching capacity. While that rating sounds robust on paper, automotive engineering rarely operates at the upper limits of component ratings for high-current paths like starter circuits. To justify using a 30A deviceâor to determine if you need something even largerâyou must first understand the electrical characteristics of the "start" signal itself.

## The nature of the ignition-to-solenoid signal

The wire running from the key switch (often labeled as the "S" terminal on the starter solenoid) to the starter solenoid coil is not a main power feed. It carries the control voltage that energizes the solenoid's internal electromagnet to pull in the drive gear and engage the starter motor.

In a standard 12V system, this wire typically draws between 3A and 6A when the key is turned to the "Start" position. This current spike occurs because it must overcome the resistance of the solenoid coil and any internal contact resistance in the ignition switch before the high-current path (the battery-to-cranking motor circuit) closes.

While some modern vehicles with complex starter control modules might see slightly different draw patterns depending on whether they use a direct magnetic pull or a pre-engagement sequence, the vast majority of traditional electromagnetic solenoids fall within that 3A to 6A range. Even if your specific ignition switch has internal shunts or bypasses that momentarily alter resistance, you are rarely approaching the 10A threshold unless there is a severe short circuit or a faulty solenoid coil drawing excessive current.

## Evaluating the MAH-112-C-4 specification

The MAH-112-C-4 rating of 30A is indeed significantly higher than the typical ~5A load of an ignition-to-solenoid wire. In engineering terms, this provides a massive safety margin. However, that margin comes with trade-offs regarding physical size, cost, and installation complexity.

A relay rated for 30A will have larger internal contacts, thicker terminals, and often requires a wider mounting footprint than a standard 5A or 10A automotive relay. If your primary goal is simply to interrupt the control signal to the solenoid, a smaller relay might suffice, provided its mechanical switching speed matches the ignition cycle requirements.

However, there is a distinct advantage to using an over-specified component in high-vibration environments like under-hood applications. Larger contacts tend to weld less easily during high-current fault events, and thicker terminals reduce voltage drop across the connection points. If you choose the MAH-112-C-4, ensure your mounting hardware can handle the physical dimensions; forcing a large relay into a tight engine bay without proper clearance can lead to heat buildup or interference with moving parts like belts or hoses.

## Implementation considerations for an immobilizer setup

When integrating this relay into an immobilization system, you are essentially creating a series switch in the low-current control path. Your logic circuit (whether using a microcontroller, an Arduino, or a dedicated security module) needs to drive the coil of this new inline relay.

Since the load on your new relay is only ~5A max, you can safely use a standard 5A automotive relay for the switching element if you prefer a compact form factor. However, if you are building a custom immobilizer unit and want to utilize the MAH-112-C-4 directly, treat it as a robust switch rather than a precision component.

Be mindful of the coil voltage driving your new inline relay. Ensure your control circuit can handle the inrush current required to energize the relay coil, which is distinct from the 30A switching capacity of the contacts. A typical automotive solenoid coil might require 12V at roughly 40mA-80mA; match your driver transistor or logic gate output accordingly.

## Final verification

Before finalizing the installation, verify the actual current draw of your specific vehicle's starter solenoid coil using a clamp meter if possible. While the industry standard is low amps, aftermarket modifications or older solenoids with degraded windings can occasionally present higher resistance loads that behave unexpectedly. If you confirm the draw stays under 10A, the MAH-112-C-4 is more than adequate and will likely outlast a cheaper alternative due to its superior contact mass and thermal handling capabilities.
